query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of chromium (≈4–5 at%) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enhance its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective Cr2O3 scale during high-temperature air exposure, without compromising its inherent room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a BCC matrix exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 4–5 atomic percent chromium into the alloy composition (i.e., modify the composition to HfNbTaTiZrCr_x with x ≈ 4–5 at%).
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical testing includes room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (≈1000 °C, strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) performance evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, adherent, and continuous Cr2O3 oxide layer on the alloy surface while maintaining the favorable BCC microstructure internally.
generation.mechanism: Chromium has a high affinity for oxygen and, when added in small amounts, preferentially oxidizes to form Cr2O3. This protective oxide scale serves as an oxygen barrier that inhibits further oxidation (pesting) at elevated temperatures, while its limited volume fraction minimizes alterations to the bulk microstructure and preserves mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cr-doped alloy will show significantly reduced oxidation (lower weight gain and a uniform Cr2O3 scale) after 5 h exposure at 800 °C, while retaining room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength within the original performance window.
generation.baseline: The undoped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which, although mechanically adequate, suffers from rapid oxygen-induced degradation when exposed to high-temperature air.
generation.boundary: Results are expected under conditions of air exposure at approximately 800 °C for durations around 5 hours and mechanical testing at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (≈1000 °C, strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Cr concentration for maximizing oxidation resistance without adversely affecting phase stability or mechanical properties remains to be precisely determined, and potential interactions with existing alloying elements must be characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (baseline) and another with ~4–5 at% Cr added. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform surface characterization (SEM/EDS) to evaluate oxide scale formation and measure weight gain. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength testing at ≈1000 °C (at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹).
measurements: Weight gain and oxide scale thickness via SEM/EDS
Continuity and adherence of the Cr2O3 scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of chromium does not result in a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar weight gain and non-protective oxide morphology) or if the mechanical properties (ductility or high-temperature yield strength) degrade beyond acceptable limits compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
